en: Preface to the Categorized Essential Compendium of Miraculous Responses to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the orthodox core of the Mahāyāna. As the Tathāgata said:
"All Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas arise from this sūtra. Thus, this sūtra is the sacred teaching.

It is the marrow of my bones. Its merit is inconceivable. Those who recite it can shatter all phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and penetrate to the source of nature, reaching directly to the other shore of *nirvāṇa*.
How could it be merely a matter of various karmic rewards whose responses never fail?

Nevertheless, to clarify the Way without calculating its merit is something that only those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom might be able to achieve; as for those of middling or inferior capacity—
Those who do not perceive the retribution of blessings will find their faith unsteady; how then can they be made to delight in recitation without weariness?
Having already composed this word-by-word commentary, I have further compiled this collection categorized by spiritual responses.

Among the historical records and biographies transmitted from ancient and modern times, there are no fewer than several thousand verifiable accounts. To record them all would be tedious, and I fear that people...
It is difficult to record them all; therefore, I have selected fifty essential instances and divided them into eighteen categories.

In every case, the response was immediate upon invocation, as swift as a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound. These are truly sufficient to convert those who have not yet believed and to inspire in people a desire to recite them with joy.

One should observe that these responses also vary in degree, ranging from the shallow to the profound and the small to the great—such as the prolongation of life, the recovery from illness, the birth of children, and success in the imperial examinations.

Furthermore, matters such as escaping calamities and returning to life all result in the enjoyment of worldly blessings and retributions; these are causes of out-flowing existence (*sāsrava*) and are not what those seeking transcendence value.

Only the single practice of returning to the West can bring an end to birth and death, liberate one from saṃsāra, and lead directly to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one may gather together with all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This is truly for those who study the Way...
This is the ultimate destination. All recitation, exposition, transcription, carving for distribution, and so forth, originally seek nothing other than this.

Other various miraculous responses are merely incidental by-products. There are differences in the depth of one's merit and the magnitude of the resulting efficacy. I hope that those who peruse this compilation will cast their gaze upon the heights.
On the eighth day of the second month in the twenty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, the lay devotee Wang Zesheng,
"Guiyi," respectfully inscribed this preface for the *Classified Compendium of Essential Accounts of Miraculous Responses to the Vajracchedikā Sūtra*:
[Accounts concerning] prolonging life, curing illness, obtaining offspring, passing the examinations, avoiding drowning, and extinguishing fires.

*The Essential Compendium of Categorized Accounts of Miraculous Responses to the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: Repelling ghosts, avoiding malevolent spirits, subduing tigers, transforming bandits,
escaping calamities, returning to life from death, avoiding rebirth as an animal, fulfilling wishes, delivering birds, aiding the deceased, and ascending to heaven to return to the Western Land.
Compiled by Wang Zesheng of Penglai, Fu;
transcribed by his son-in-law Sun Tianjin and Yunqing, for the benefit of Yan Shou.
During the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Dharma Master Yan resided at the Zhaoti Monastery in Chang’an. He had entered the monastic order at the age of eleven.
One day, he encountered a physiognomist who said to him, “It is a pity that despite your intelligence, your life will be short; your lifespan is exhausted at eighteen years.

Yan returned home, burned incense, paid homage to the Triple Gem, and made a vow, requesting that he be granted a single scroll of scripture which he might receive and uphold with focused devotion. Having finished his prayers, he reached out and drew one from his hand.
This scroll is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He devoted himself single-mindedly to its recitation and upholding, never ceasing day or night.

Suddenly, late one night when the hour was deep, he saw five-colored light appear within his room. In a brief moment, he beheld a Brahman monk, five feet tall, who said to Yan: "You were destined to die at eighteen;
however, due to the merit of your recitation of this Mahāyāna sūtra, your lifespan has been extended. Having spoken, the monk vanished. Consequently...
He redoubled his diligent practice. Later, when he reached the age of ninety-two, he passed away peacefully while sitting in meditation without illness.

During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty, Wu Si-huan served as a Doctor of the Imperial Academy. He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twice daily and experienced many miraculous responses.
While Si-huan was ill in the capital, there was a sorcerer named Chu Xi-er who could divine matters with god-like accuracy through astrology and divination. He performed prayers and rites for him...
Sīxuán prayed. Sīxuán went to see Sīxiān, who asked in surprise, "What incantations do you possess? When ghosts see them, they all flee.
Sīxuán realized this was the power of the scripture and his faith became even more diligent; he recited it five times every day. His elder brother fell ill, and the physicians were ineffective.
Sīxuán recited the scripture with a sincere heart, and after three days, his brother recovered. Once, at the Wei Bridge, Sīxuán saw an elderly man over eighty years of age.
He was wearing mourning clothes of hempen cloth. When asked why, he replied, "It is for my biological mother. Si Xuan found this strange and questioned him further.
He answered, "My mother was forty-three years old when a strange monk instructed her, saying: 'If you wish for longevity, simply recite the Diamond Sutra.

From the day she resolved her mind upon this, she recited it twice daily. She lived to the age of one hundred and seven. Her aunt and a neighbor’s mother also recited it, and both exceeded the age of one hundred."
In Jiangling, there was a man named Li Xuanzong. His daughter, thirteen years of age, dreamed of a *bhikṣu* who said to her: "You possess a virtuous mind;

why do you not recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? If men and women of this world can daily recite one fascicle with a pure mind, their blessings and longevity will increase in the world of the living, and they shall live out a full hundred years before passing away, at which point they will be reborn in the celestial realms. If they can thoroughly master the *Prajñā*, [the merit is even greater]."
She ascended directly to the other shore of Nirvana. There were also those who had not yet finished reading the sutras;

when they died and entered the underworld, they could not be detained or recorded, but were instead judged to be reborn into wealthy and noble families to receive various blessings and rewards. Following the monk’s instructions, the girl Li recited three fascicles daily.
At the age of twenty-four, she refused to marry. Suddenly afflicted with a case of *shanghan* (typhoid fever), she passed away after three days. Two messengers led her [away].

Upon seeing King Yama, he was examined and found that his daughter was innocent. Seeing a halo of Buddha-light upon her head, the King said, "Since this girl possesses the merit of Prajñā, it is fitting to decree her restoration to life.
As she was about to depart, the King instructed her, saying, "Your father harbors a grudge against you for the crime of murder."

First, his lifespan was reduced by two *jì* (twenty-four years). Before long, he was summoned to the Office of the Shades for interrogation. Your father had a fondness for cutting up live fish for sashimi;
now there are more than seven thousand fish who have filed a formal complaint seeking his life. Every night, your father dreams that he has fallen into a fishing net.
Every day he suffered from headaches; this was because the fish was seeking retribution. The daughter returned to life and informed her father of this.
The father was filled with alarm, so he went with his daughter to Tianning Temple to provide a vegetarian feast for one hundred monks and vowed to renounce meat and wine.

He personally transcribed forty-nine fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon its completion, Emperor Xuanzong dreamed at night that several thousand youths dressed in green came to pay their respects.
He replied, "I prostrate. We were about to be slaughtered by you, each of us recounting our grievances from past lives and demanding your life.

Now, through the merit of your copying of the sutras, we have escaped the sufferings of the three evil realms and been reborn in the good paths. Since you have released us from our enmity, we restore your original lifespan and grant you further longevity.
When the Emperor Xuanzong heard this, he was filled with boundless joy. From that time on, he never ceased reciting the sutras, and his life was prolonged.
He reached the age of one hundred and twenty and passed away without illness.

During the Zhengde era of the Ming dynasty, there was a great virtuous monk at Mount Nanyue named Chushi. He was extensively learned in the Tripitaka and specialized in the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Whenever anyone paid him respects or requested the Buddha-dharma—regardless of whether they were wise or foolish, noble or humble—he would immediately call out in a loud voice:
"Go, uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with diligence. He passed away at the age of one hundred and seventy-one.
At that same time, there were the monks Baiteng and Wuji, who also specialized in exhorting others to uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Baiteng lived to the age of one hundred and thirty, and Wuji lived to the age of one hundred and twenty-four.

Yu Ji was the son of Wang Cheng. His family resided in Jinzhou. By nature he was stubborn and base. In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, his family was struck by a plague and perished;
only Ji happened to escape. During the illness, he ate dog meat, and his eyes consequently became blind. He sought no medical treatment, praying instead to ghosts and spirits for several days.
For years there was no response. Suddenly, a strange monk appeared and requested a meal, saying to him, "The Diamond Sūtra can dispel all sufferings;
can you, Layman, accept it? Huicheng declined on the grounds that he was blind. The monk urged him to have it transcribed, and Huicheng followed his advice, obtaining seven fascicles.
He requested a monk to recite [the scripture] for several days, after which he dreamed of the aforementioned monk holding a blade and cutting open his eyes. He was startled awake;
upon waking, he saw something, and after a long time, his vision returned to clarity. From then on, he recited the sutras for the rest of his life without ceasing.
Goulong Yi was a native of Jianzhou. During the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, he worked as a hired laborer in Qixian County.

Once, while visiting a fellow villager who was ill, he saw that the man was copying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Yi tore it up and forbade him from continuing. Upon returning home, Yi suddenly became mute; no physician could cure him.
For five or six years, he remained stubborn, dull-witted, and devoid of consciousness. Suddenly, he heard a neighbor reciting this very sūtra, and he was struck with a sense of alarm.
He said, "I previously slandered the True Sutra and incurred this muteness. If I now repent and apologize, pledging to venerate it for the rest of my life, would you be able to speak again?
From then on, whenever he heard the chanting of sutras, he would lean against the wall to listen. After more than a month, he happened to enter a temple while walking.

He encountered an elderly monk and paid him homage. The monk asked what he needed, to which [the man] pointed to his mouth and acted out being mute. The monk used a knife to cut beneath his tongue, whereupon he was able to speak.
He then recited a scripture with him, and it matched the voice of his neighbor exactly. Later, when he went to visit the monk again, the monk was nowhere to be seen;
there was only a painting of Subhūti on the wall. He then realized, "This is he. Consequently, whenever he transcribed a scripture, he would paint a figure of Subhūti.
[He] made an image [of the Buddha] and worshipped it for the rest of his life.
The retired scholar of Kunshan, Zhou Shaoyue, whose name was Zhicheng, lost his sight at age fifty; his pupils were turned backward and were blue in color.

Considering himself a person of failed potential, he turned his heart toward the Buddha to extinguish his past transgressions. Every morning at dawn, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in three fascicles;
when reciting, he would chant aloud with praise. He did not offer formal greetings to guests who arrived. Fifteen years passed, and one day he suddenly saw objects with vivid clarity.
Yet, because he was blind, he could not see them, believing it to be a manifestation of deluded thoughts. Nevertheless, he caused others to look.
As for his eyesight: having already seen the boy’s eyes flicker, after two months the clear light was fully restored. Compared to his youth, he could see even further into the distance.
Moved by the power of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Shaoyue held the scripture with increasing devotion. When he reached the age of eighty, he passed away peacefully.
During the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, Song Chengxin of Xiuzhou suffered from a case of reversed stomach (upward-moving qi) that could not be cured by medicine for several years.

Suddenly, one night he dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said to him, "This present illness and suffering of yours are caused by karmic enmity and transgressions from your past lives; do you understand?"

Generally, among the men and women of the world, those who are paralyzed, afflicted with consumption, lame, blind, deaf, mute, or whose bodies are entangled by disease such that they have lain upon their beds for years,
their spirits are mostly apprehended by the authorities of the underworld to be interrogated regarding the evil deeds they committed in their previous lives and the present one.

The relationship between cause and effect does not deviate by even a hair’s breadth. If there is one who reverently offers the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whether copying it themselves or for others, or upholding it throughout their entire life, as soon as they form this thought, the deities of the underworld will immediately respond and examine their meritorious deeds. First, they shall release the person's soul;

next, they shall encounter a skilled physician, and the illness will be cured. Upon waking and attaining realization, they should burn incense the following morning and personally make vows before the Buddha.

He was granted one thousand copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Subsequently, he again dreamed of the Vajra Deity, who bestowed upon him a medicinal pill and instructed him to swallow it.
On the following day, his illness was immediately cured. After nursing himself for over a month, his physical strength returned to its former state. All who saw or heard of this—
Everyone praised him without exception.
He fathered a son, Pu Kechong, who was a student at the Xiushui School. His wife, surnamed Wang, had one son and one daughter, both of whom died of smallpox in succession; he wept for them.

His grief was so excessive that both his eyes became blind. He then devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, continuing for several years without ceasing.
One day, while in the midst of reciting the sutra, his left eye suddenly began to flow with tears; it felt as though it were being cut and torn apart, yet then it suddenly became clear.
After several days, the same occurred with his right eye. Consequently, his recitation became even more devout. One night, he dreamed that the Buddha spoke to him, saying: "You originally had no..."
Because of his recitation of the scriptures, [the deity] granted him a son; he was named Jingci (Scripture-Gifted). Shi Zhenyu was a native of Yinxian.

By nature he loved to do good, yet after his age exceeded forty, he had no son. He paid homage to Master Miyun of Tiantong, who gave him the name Tongdeng (Equal to the Way) and instructed him, saying:
"If you wish to obtain an heir, you must observe the fast for the monks and uphold the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. From then on...
However, he had a son. That night, following these instructions, he prostrated before the Buddha and made a vow; he then dreamed of the Vajra Deity, who gave him a single character, "Zhao" (兆).

Upon returning home, he immediately began a vegetarian diet and personally transcribed one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reciting it with devotion every day without fail through both cold and heat.
Year after year, she entered the mountains to offer vegetarian feasts and performed various acts of merit with tireless diligence. Subsequently, she indeed bore five sons.
During the Shunzhi era of the Qing Dynasty, General Zhang Gongming Jie, the Commander-in-Chief of Zhejiang, was sixty years old and still without an heir.
Lady Chen was a devoted believer in the Triple Gem; she recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily and traveled to every famous mountain to offer vegetarian feasts.
In the second month of the fifth year of the Kangxi era, she performed the *Avataṃsaka Repentance Ritual* at Tiantong Temple, where seven days of five-colored clouds appeared over the mountains.
In the seventh month of that autumn, her secondary wife gave birth to a son. Her family has maintained her final instructions to this day. They revere...
The Buddha recited the sutras without ceasing.

During the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Yang Xun served as the Judicial Commissioner of Kuizhou; he constantly upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and maintained a straightforward mind in his conduct. In secret...
Debochuan had a son who was twenty-three years old. He was studying for the civil service examinations and was about to enter the test center.
Ten days prior, he dreamed one night that the Vajra Deity said to him, "Your recitation of the sutras has moved the spirits; I have come specifically to inform you that your son will surely be noble.

If he is to take the examination, you must change his name to Yang Chun before submitting his application. I shall assist him with my pen during the exam. The following day, he ordered his son to change his name and submit his examination papers.

He was sixth among his peers in the examination results. The following year, he went to take the provincial examination. During the night, Chūn dreamed of a Vajrapāṇi deity who said to him, "The provincial essay topic this year will be:

'Walking the Royal Way and Becoming a King. You should prepare for your entry into the examination hall in advance and keep this secret. On the day of the examination, it turned out that the topic was exactly as predicted, and he ranked ninety-sixth.
He then proceeded to the palace examination, which concluded with the examiners selecting the top three candidates. Chūn was one of them.
The scroll was presented to the imperial dais. That night, Chun again dreamed that the former deity said to him, "Your composition is excellent, yet it does not accord with the examiner's intent;
it has been placed in the fifth volume. I have already sought out your true scroll and have gone to the imperial dais to replace the first-place candidate’s paper with it.
When the names are called on the following day, you shall be determined as the Grand Champion of the empire. This is because you are my companion."
His father had long reflected upon the efficacy of the *Zhujing* (True Scriptures). When the names were called, the response was indeed as expected.
Xiang Hixian, the Vice-Censor-in-Chief, whose original name was Decha, dreamed that he had been selected for the Xinhao year provincial examination;

however, because he had defiled two young maidservants, his name was struck from the list of successful candidates by a divine being. Thereupon, he diligently practiced deeds of sowing merit and donated funds to entreat his friends [to intercede].
Kōmatsu Shō devoted himself to carving woodblocks for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and offered them annually for over ten years.

One night, he dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where he saw a yellow paper with the eighth name listed as "Item" (Kō), with the middle character blurred and the bottom character as "Gen" (Gen).
A person standing beside him said, "Examine this closely; it is your rank on the Celestial Register. Consequently, he changed his name to Mōgen. In the year of Renzi, he traveled north.
In the provincial examination, he ranked twenty-ninth; in the metropolitan examination of the Jiwu year, he was third. Everyone marveled at the discrepancy between his dream and his actual ranking.

However, in the palace examination, he became second, and in the final imperial examination, he was fifth. Only then did he realize that these positions corresponded exactly to the eighth place in the sequence of the "Three Excellencies" (the top three ranks).
Furthermore, while the placards of the provincial examination were all white, those of the palace examination were uniquely yellow—this too was clearly a matter of divine ordainment.

Regarding "Jiahe": When Shen Gong Guanghua was serving as the Salt and Iron Commissioner for the Two Huais, on the day he retired to his fields, he happened to be sitting idly with his fellow provincial official, Transport Commissioner Wu Gong Song.
They conversed at ease, taking turns to ask one another what they had been doing during the day. Shen said, "In the morning, I observed the vegetarian fast."
Wu had been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for twenty years, having already completed more than two *piṭakas*. Wu, however, had treated it with indifference.
Not long after, Wu suddenly rose at dawn and hurried off to congratulate Shen, saying, "The young master will certainly pass the Southern Examination.
When Shen asked why he said this, Wu replied, "I dreamed of a man who said that a certain scholar in our district, by virtue of his merit from reciting the *Vajracchedikā*, would succeed."

His son obtained a distinguished success. Upon waking, he thought only of Master Gong’s dream that he should repay him for it. That autumn, Shen Gong Shuzi passed the provincial examination for the Imperial University.
It was heard that Master Shen was most devout in his recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, being able to recite it from memory while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
He once traveled back and forth from the home of Ji Zi of the Eastern Suburb; along the way, one—

He maintained the recitation in his mind. Calculating those who passed through the butcher markets and stalls, as well as all those throughout space who were liberated by the merit of this sutra, one cannot know how many there were.

Furthermore, because he cultivated all wholesome dharmas with a mind free from the four marks (*catur-nimitta*) and accumulated merit over successive lifetimes, his descendants have maintained their lineage through the imperial examinations and constitute the preeminent clan of Hezhou; these are all said to be the verified manifestations of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Miani was from Jiujiang during the Yuan dynasty. He sold firewood in the market and was seventy years old. He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
One day, while crossing the river, a current arose in midstream; those crossing with him all drowned, but Miani alone floated upon the water and drifted to the southern bank. A crowd...

Those who had moored their boats were all greatly astonished. Seeing that a light several feet high emanated from the back of the man at the prow, they took him for a person of noble rank and vied with one another to offer him clothes and provide him with food.
As they conversed more intimately, they learned he was but a village elder; they then questioned him about the source of the light.

He replied, "I have recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for ten years. The scripture is upon my back; through it, there has been no calamity or hardship from which I have not been delivered."

Bai Renzhe served as the Magistrate of Laiyang during the Longshuo era. While transporting grain to Liaodong, he encountered a storm at sea; the four directions became pitch black, and Renzhe was struck with fear.
He urgently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and suddenly, as if in a dream, he saw a brahmin monk who said to him:
"Because you have kept the True Sutra in mind, I have come to rescue you. In an instant, the wind subsided, and more than eighty people were all saved.
During the Qiannian era of the Tang dynasty, the monk Qianhui of Guangzhou had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since childhood, never ceasing regardless of cold or heat.
Once, while traveling by sea with several dozen monastics and laypeople toward Nan'an, they were suddenly struck by a tempest that wrecked their ship; everyone on board—
He was lost at sea. Only Qianhui remained amidst the waves when he encountered a thicket of weeds that caught against his body.

He gradually rose to the top of the weeds and drifted with the current for three days and nights before finally reaching shore. Upon examining the weeds closely, he found within them a single copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

There was no dampness or moisture at all. Qianhui reverently received this scripture and made offerings with sincere devotion. When he reached the age of one hundred and thirty, he sat upright and passed away.
From within the scripture itself, fragrant smoke emerged, gradually forming clouds of five colors that slowly ascended into the sky.
The fires were brought under control at Ráozhōu. There were over ten thousand households of silver miners, all of whom lived in thatched huts. During the Yányán era, a fire broke out;

the ten thousand dwellings were all reduced to ashes, yet within only one household did the flames fail to reach. At that time, Yang Tíjǐ of the local commandery personally questioned an old man. The old man—
A person replied: "My family serves the Buddha and merely recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. It was this scripture that repelled the ghosts.
Wei Xun, the son of Shangde, the Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary, served as the Great General of the Guard at the Gatekeeper’s Post; he too held the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At that time, there was Cai Ce, who died suddenly. After several days, he revived and said: "I arrived at the Netherworld Office.

The officials were about to flog the messengers because they could not find the person they were supposed to pursue. The messengers said, 'Wei Xun holds the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and he is protected by benevolent deities; therefore, we cannot find him.
They immediately dispatched other messengers to pursue him again, but after a short while, their reports were identical. The Netherworld Official said, 'Cease the pursuit for now. Wei Xun.
Upon hearing this, he redoubled his diligent practice.

During the Tang dynasty, Wang Ta served as a *guoyi* (commander) of the Eagle-Flight Command (*Yingyang Fu*). Due to illness, he subsequently abstained from pungent meats and resolved to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* five times daily.
Later, when he contracted a severe illness and saw a host of ghosts approaching, Ta immediately recited the sutra; upon hearing it, the ghosts retreated. From afar...
He said, "The King has ordered you to be pursued; stop for a moment and recite the sutra. As Da-xie recited, the ghosts all moved forward toward him, and he consequently fell into a stupor.
After a short while, he saw another ghost who said, "O reciter of the sutra, the King has granted you a temporary reprieve of six months.

Upon awakening, he then devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation, never ceasing day or night. When the six months had passed, the ghosts did not come again. At night, he heard a voice calling out from the air:
"By virtue of your merit in upholding this sutra, you shall live for ninety years.
During the Zhenguan era, Shen Jiahui of the Tang dynasty served as a Proofreader (Jiaoshu lang). On official business, he was assigned to Lanzhou; his longing to return home was most intense.
Every morning and evening, he faced east and prostrated before Mount Tai, praying that he might return alive.

On the third day of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Yonghui era, he saw a youth at night whose appearance and attire were most elegant. The youth said he was the son of the Lord of Mount Tai and thanked him for his prostrations.
Therefore, he was sent to welcome [the monk]. He said to Jiahui, "When a person commits evil, they may not be executed while alive, but after death they will certainly be punished by the ghosts;

there is no way to escape this through mere luck. If you recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* once every day, then all ten thousand offenses will be extinguished, and the ghost officials will be unable to detain you.
From that time on, Jiahui maintained the practice of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and upon encountering a general amnesty, he was released.

Upon returning home, he avoided the Tang capital and went to see Li Miàn. During the Yuanhe era, as he was about to return home after failing the jinshi examination, a monk exhorted him, saying: "Young master..."
Desiring to pass the imperial examination, he thought, "Why not recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? He subsequently recited it several dozen times every day.

Upon arriving at Wangqiao to stay the night, he was walking in the moonlight when he saw a beautiful woman. He spoke with her and was enticed to a village house, where they laughed and joked very boisterously.

When he ascended into the hall, he saw five or six more beautiful women. Returning home, he suspected it had been a strange apparition and secretly recited the sutra; suddenly, a wondrous light emerged from [the text].

As she spoke, the women fled in terror, smelling only a foul, carrion-like stench; it was clearly the dwelling of foxes and wild beasts. Thorns and brambles filled their view, and they did not know where to go.
Suddenly, a white dog appeared and led them back forward, its mouth emitting light that illuminated the path. Thus, they reached their original location.
Afterward, she recited the sutras until she had reached several tens of thousands of repetitions.
Tang of Fuhu.

In Shishou County, there was a śrāmaṇera named Daoyin who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At the beginning of the Changqing era, he was returning home at night from elsewhere when he encountered a tiger on the road.
The tiger roared and lunged forward; the śrāmaṇera then closed his eyes and sat, silently reciting the sutra. The tiger subsequently crouched down and submitted.
He guarded it like grass until dawn, when he finally departed. Looking at the spot where he had crouched, he saw that saliva had flowed onto the ground.

During the Tang dynasty, Wang Lingwang, who had maintained the practice of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since his youth, was returning to Qiongzhou. The road was extremely perilous and obstructed, when he suddenly encountered a fierce beast.
When he encountered an extraordinary calamity while traveling through the marshes, he urgently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. A fierce beast dragged its tail and departed.

Later, while serving as the Assistant Administrator (*Panshi*) of Anzhou, he crossed the Yangzi River at night when a violent storm arose; hundreds of ships were all submerged, yet only the boat from which Li Wang was looking on remained intact.
Huàzé Táng (化賊唐).
During the early years of the Chángqìng era, there was a man from Shǎnzhōu named Qián Xínglì who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Wherever he went, he would burn incense and pay homage to it. Once, while transporting goods toward Tóngzhōu, he encountered bandits on the road. Xínglì abandoned his merchandise and fled; his belongings were [seized]. Five...

It weighed sixty jin. When the thief tried to lift it, he could not move it. Looking at one another in astonishment, they followed him and questioned him. He replied, "There is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* within it;

I suspect this is its supernatural power. The thief opened the bag and saw the scripture. He instead gave Li one hundred thousand coins and requested the scripture, vowing never to commit theft again.
During the Sui dynasty, there was a magistrate of Wulao County named Lu Yantong, who recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* ten scrolls daily.
When Li Mi’s rebellion broke out and the city was captured, a band of rebels pursued him with swords. As they drew near a deep ravine, Yantong leaped into it and emerged unharmed.
In the midst [of the ordeal], he saw a Vajra deity who reached out his hand to join with the monk’s arm and placed it upon the stone; the arm suffered no injury whatsoever.
The deity said, "Your recitation of this sutra has moved me, and I have come specifically to save you. Because of this, you have been preserved and shall return home.
He then took up his brush and wrote a verse, bathed in scented water, and passed away while sitting upright.

During the Tang dynasty, there was a wealthy merchant who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He always carried the scripture with him wherever he went. Once, while traveling abroad for trade, he stayed overnight on a sea island.

The other merchants, coveting his wealth, murdered him, placed his body in a large wicker basket, weighted it down with a massive stone, and sank both the basket and the scripture into the sea before departing.
The island where they had sunk them was actually a monastery; every evening, the monks there would hear the sound of someone reciting the sutra.

At the bottom of the sea, they were greatly astonished. Consequently, they ordered a skilled swimmer to dive into the water to search for him. There he saw an old man reading a scripture inside a cage;
he then pulled and dragged him up. When the monk asked for the reason, the man said: "I was killed and cast into the sea, yet I did not realize I was in a cage.
Suddenly, I became aware that my body was in a palace, where people constantly brought me food and drink, and I lived in peace, comfort, and freedom. When the assembly heard this, they were moved.
Everyone praised him with admiration. He subsequently shaved his hair and left home to enter a monastery on an island.

Lu Kangcheng of the Tang dynasty once served as a clerk in the Office of Law (*faco*). Being one who did not shrink from confronting the powerful or the oppressive, he would suddenly see a deceased official after retiring from his duties.

This official was carrying several hundred scrolls of documents and petitions, requesting Lu’s signature. Lu asked, "You have already passed away; how is it that you can come here? The official replied, "This is the Netherworld Court."
The official documents were examined by Kangcheng. They contained only names and lacked almost any other information. The clerk said, "These are all those who will die by the blade next year.
He then asked, "Am I among them? The clerk replied, "Yes. He was greatly alarmed and said, "Since you are a veteran official, could you not save me?
The clerk said, "I have come specifically to inform you; only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* can be entrusted to you. Having finished speaking, he immediately—

He did not see [the scripture]. Thereupon, Kāng-ch'eng resolved to read the sūtra, reciting it dozens of times each day. The following year, Zhu Ch'i rebelled; he indeed appointed Kāng-ch'eng as a Censor.
Kāng-ch'eng rebuked Ch'i, saying, "A rebel minister dares to interfere with a man of national caliber! Ch'i was enraged and ordered his soldiers to surround him and shoot at him.
Kāng-ch'eng silently recited the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the Diamond Sūtra), and none of the arrows caused him harm. Ch'i said, "The Confucian takes loyalty and good faith as..."
"His armor! It is true! Having said this, he abandoned his post. Kang Cheng subsequently entered Zhongnan Mountain and never again served in office.
Xiang Lanzhai was serving as a regional commander when he said: "In the spring of the Bingchen year, I dreamed that I had an audience with His Majesty the Invincible Great King.

I saw ten thousand people of a blood-stained, sickly complexion, who said, 'These are the two [regions of] Dong; you must recognize them. Upon returning, I urged people to observe the fast and maintain a vegetarian diet, and to recite..."
If one recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one may be spared from the calamities of war while alive, and after death, be delivered from suffering and distress.
Not long after, several prefectures in Shandong suffered a great famine; those who died were nearly all of them, and as the situation in Liaodong collapsed, the number of deaths doubled.
Thus, the two dreams regarding the East were proven true. Xiang Qian held the *Vajracchedikā* in his hands and never ceased reciting it for even a single day.

Huan Yang Muzong Wen-ce was a man of the Sui dynasty who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and abstained from alcohol and meat. In the seventh year of the Daye era, he died suddenly;
three days later, he returned to life. Initially, he saw two ghosts who pursued him to a city that was extremely imposing and stern. He entered and walked through its four gates.
Five *li* away, he saw a palace with a retinue of guards. The King sat upon the throne, surrounded by monks, Daoists, and people from the four barbarian quarters in numbers beyond counting.
The messenger entered the audience chamber with the written record (*wen-ce*) behind him. One by one, the King questioned them regarding their good and evil deeds during their lifetimes.

They were divided into two groups facing east and west; then the King called out the names from the record and asked, "What good deeds did you perform? He replied, "Since my youth, I have upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King joined his palms and sighed in praise.
He said, "The merit is exceedingly great; let him go free.
During the early years of the Changqing era, the monk Fazheng of Kaiyuan Temple in Jiangling, Tang China, recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* thirty-seven times every day.

He died suddenly. Upon reaching the Netherworld, he was presented before the King. The King asked what meritorious deeds he had performed during his lifetime. He replied, "I constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Thereupon, the King gestured for him to ascend the hall; he climbed the embroidered throne and recited the sutra. All the attendants joined their palms in reverence, and the tortures being inflicted below the steps all ceased.
When the recitation was finished, an official was sent to lead him back. As the King descended the steps to see him off, he said, "The Master shall further attain three [more lifetimes]..."
He remained among humans for ten years, never ceasing his recitation and study. Later, while traveling with an official, they came upon a great pit.
The official pushed him from behind; as he fell into the void, he revived. He had been dead for seven days, yet only his face was not cold.

During the Wude era, there was Su Renqin of Chang’an. His father, Wenzhong, was a man of immense wealth who charged interest at fivefold rates, used oversized bushels and undersized scales, and took life and harmed living beings without a single thought toward goodness. He died by falling into a latrine in his old age.
Renqin was no different from his father; relying on his wealth, he cheated others and slaughtered animals at will. Before he had reached the age of thirty, a grave illness suddenly arose.
When one is ill, one sees sentient beings at one's side demanding one's life; when dying, one sees Lord Yama, who issues a decree:
"Because you cultivated goodness in your previous lives, you have received blessings in this present life. Yet now, you have indulged in killing and slaughter, failing to recognize cause and effect.

Therefore, I order the jailers to drive you to the Mountains of Knives and the Forests of Swords to repay the lives of sentient beings. Qin then pleaded in distress: "While I was in the world, although I did not read the sutras or perform [meritorious deeds]..."
"Excellent! Previously, you offered wealth to request a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which you then gave to the monk Shenjing of Anguo Temple for him to uphold.
Now that this monk has passed away, how could there not be a karmic response? In an instant, Shenjing appeared before the King, holding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in his hands."

It is said that Qin once bestowed scriptures and made vows based on the merit of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Consequently, he was allowed to return to life. The King immediately joined his palms and released him to go back.

After Qin revived, he printed and distributed one hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and one thousand fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and performed the Great Water-Land Feast (*shuilu daizhai*).
While he was performing various meritorious deeds, his deceased father suddenly appeared in a dream at night and said, "I have been undergoing immeasurable suffering in hell.
Now, because of your cultivation and by relying on the power of the Buddha, I and the spirits of my ancestors for seven generations have all been reborn in the heavenly realms."

During the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Tian, who served as a military aide (*canjun*) in Yizhou. He took great pleasure in hunting. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, while releasing hawks in a thicket, he saw a scroll of a book atop a thorn bush.
Upon picking it up and examining it, he found it to be the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. From that time on, he resolved to recite it;

after several years, he had already recited it more than two thousand times. Nevertheless, he did not cease his hunting. Later, he fell ill and died suddenly, whereupon he was summoned to the underworld.
The Prefect saw various birds and beasts circling for several mu around him, begging for their lives. Shortly thereafter, he saw the King, who asked why his karmic offenses were so numerous.
Tian was unable to answer. The King ordered an investigation. Ten of his companions arrived at the magistrate’s office;

the magistrates joined their mouths together, and by throwing a single pill into each mouth, they were instantly transformed into blazing fires. In a moment, their entire bodies were reduced to ashes, yet immediately they were restored once more.

There were six or seven such individuals. When it came to Mr. Tian, he stacked three pellets [of incense] without showing any sign of fire. The officials found this strange and reported the facts in full.
The King asked him what meritorious deeds he had performed while alive. Tian replied, "During my life, I recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* more than two thousand times.
The King said, "That is sufficient to extinguish all sins," and then ordered Mr. Tian to recite the scripture. Hardly had he begun...

Three sheets [of paper]. When he looked back at the birds and beasts in the courtyard, they were no longer to be seen. Having finished reciting it, the King praised him, saying, "By reciting this three thousand times, one's lifespan will be extended by fifteen years. He was then released and returned home.
During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, an official named Zhang—whose personal name has been lost—was serving as an envoy to Huainan.
As he was about to cross the Huai River, a man dressed in yellow garments came running up from behind, seeking a place on his boat. The boatman wished to cast him out, but Zhang said, "It cannot be;
what hardship is there in carrying one commoner across the river? Seeing that the man in yellow was hungry, Zhang fed him with his remaining food. The man...
He apologized for his intrusion. Once they had crossed, he took his leave of Zhang and proceeded on his way. In a short while, he arrived at the post station; the man was already there at the gate.
Zhang felt a sense of resentment and said, "I have just ferried you across; why have you come back again? The man replied, "I wish to discuss certain matters with the Magistrate;
these are not for your attendants to hear. Zhang cleared away his attendants. The man said, "I have received orders to take you; you shall drown in the Huai River."
"I am about to die. Having just received your great kindness, I can only ask for one more day. Zhang prostrated himself and begged for help.
The man replied, "If you can recite the *Juzuming Jing* (Sūtra of Prolonging Life) one thousand times within a single day, your life may yet be extended. Having said this, he departed immediately.

Upon reaching his gate, the man returned and asked, "Do you know the *Juzuming Jing*? It is none other than the *Jingang Jing* (Diamond Sūtra) found among humans. Zhang replied, "It is already late today."
"How can one complete a thousand scrolls? He replied, "Anyone who can turn them may do so. Zhang then summoned dozens of his own laborers to turn the scrolls together.
By evening, they had indeed finished the thousand scrolls. The ghost arrived again and said, "The Judge has been exempted, but you must pay a visit to the King of Hell.
When the group saw Zhang, they followed him along with the yellow-robed officials. Upon seeing the King, the King said:
By reciting this scripture, his lifespan shall be increased by ten years; he was released and reborn, spared from being a beast in Song Suzhou Prefecture.
There was a Zhu, a licentiate, who studied for the civil service examinations and was ignorant of the Buddha-dharma. One day, while wandering at leisure, he arrived at—

At Huqiu Temple, he encountered Chan Master Foyin, who was lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When the master reached the four lines beginning with "All conditioned phenomena," he explained the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma to him.
Upon hearing this, Zhu was overjoyed; he thought to himself that during his daily life he had never before heard such teachings of the Buddha-dharma.
That afternoon, after returning home, he fell asleep and dreamed of a ghost official escorting five criminals, and Zhu followed along with them. Approximately...
After walking for about a *li*, he reached a main street and entered an alley. At one house, a green curtain hung at the door;
a ghost official lifted the curtain and led the sinner inside. They arrived at a kitchen where there was hot water in a bucket atop the stove.

All the sinners drank it, and Zhu also felt thirsty and was just about to drink when the official shouted, "Those who listen to the Buddha's Dharma must not drink this! Zhu then woke up in a start, wondering if this had been a dream.
The next day, he went to the main street and entered an alley. Indeed, there was a house, no different from what he had seen in his dream. He knocked on the door and entered;
when the master of the house saw that the jinshi had arrived, he hurriedly received him. Zhu asked, "What activity was there in the kitchen at the residence just now?"

The master said, "I have been raising six small dogs in my kitchen, and one of them has died. Zhu was greatly startled and broke into a sweat, saying to himself, "Had it not been for the power of hearing the Buddha-dharma, I would almost have entered the womb of a dog.
Thereupon, he held to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without ceasing through both cold and heat.
His lifespan reached eighty-nine years. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, he invited all his teachers and friends to see him off as he ascended to the afterlife.

At the treetops of the garden, he recited a four-line verse and took his leave of the assembly. Standing upright, he passed away through transformation. The verse says: "Eighty-nine years, Master Zhu;
With both hands, he split asunder the void; With both feet, he trod upon the white clouds; He passed away standing, to the east of the Bodhi tree."
Zou Ye lived on Mount Kunshan; his family had enjoyed a reputation for goodness for generations. Ye’s younger brother, Zhen, did not practice virtuous deeds.

One day, he saw his elder brother inviting a monk to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When the recitation reached the fifteenth section, Zhen also joined his palms and remarked, "This kind of speech has never been found among us Confucians.
Later, he suffered from a seasonal illness and lost consciousness of his surroundings; for half a month, only the area of his chest remained warm.
Suddenly starting up on his bed, he told his family members: "Outside the Chang Gate, I saw a white ox belonging to the Li workshop owner.
A Vajrapāṇi deity said to me, 'This man has recited several sections of the Diamond Sūtra; how can he be among this class [of beings]?
He struck the ox's head with his precious vajra-pestle until it woke up. I felt a slight pain at the crown of my head. Later, he went to visit him.
In his household, a white calf was born, which subsequently died. As he had wished, Lü Wenzhan,

serving as the Assistant Magistrate of Langzhong County in the third year of the Kaiyuan era, possessed a refined appreciation for Buddhist scriptures and devoted himself particularly to their recitation.

He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* more than thirty thousand times. His spiritual responses were extraordinary and marvelous. As he grew old and his years declined, all three of his front teeth fell out.
Through earnest recitation and prayer, his teeth grew back as they were before. During a time of severe drought, the Provincial Governor Liu Jun ordered him to pray for rain;

after he recited the sutra once, copious rain was obtained. Later, during a period of heavy flooding, the Vice-Governor commissioned him to pray for clear weather; it cleared immediately upon his response.
There have been numerous such verifications throughout history.

Regarding the deliverance of birds during the Gengyin year of the Wanli era: there was an elderly man in Huailin Town, Huzhou, who recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as his daily practice.

In that household, there was a brooding hen that had laid twelve eggs. One night, the old man dreamed of twelve boys and girls bowing beneath the hall and saying, "We rely upon the sound of your recitation of the scriptures to enable us all to attain liberation from our avian state; we have come to express our gratitude.

Upon waking from the dream, the old man happened to think of the twelve chicken eggs. He took them out and found them to be very light; when he split them open, they were seen to be empty shells. Thereupon, he called out to the others.

They were brought forward for inspection; when they were split open, both were found to be exactly as described. Thus, those born from eggs attained liberation. Such was the spiritual efficacy [of the scripture]. This was true for all twelve classes of beings.
One can truly believe that the merit of upholding this sutra is inconceivable.

During the Jiajing and Longqing eras, the great general Qi Jiguang was a long-time practitioner of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. While he was stationed in Yue, a deceased soldier appeared to him in a dream and said:
"Tomorrow, I shall send my wife to you to beg that you recite one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā* to provide merit for her in the afterlife."
Master Dao-gong awoke and instructed his gatekeeper: "If a woman comes, do not scold or forbid her. Shortly thereafter, a woman indeed arrived, weeping piteously as she requested an audience.

He had her led inside, and she spoke exactly as she had in her dream. Master Gong granted her request. The following day, while he was reciting the sutra, he dreamed that the deceased said: "I am grateful for your great kindness;
yet I have obtained only half a scroll of merit, because the middle of it was interspersed with the two characters 'not used' (bù yòng). Master Gong—"
He pondered the reason for this. It was likely because while he was reciting the sutra, a maidservant sent by the palace ladies had delivered tea and cakes;

the Master saw her from afar, waved his hand to dismiss her, and although he did not speak, his heart felt that they were unnecessary. Thereupon, he devoted himself with utmost sincerity, closed the door, and continued his recitation. When he finished reciting, [he opened the door].
That night, he passed away in his dreams. Bowing his head, he expressed his gratitude, saying, "I have already attained transcendence.
Sheng Zai-de of Fengqiao Bridge in Suzhou received the scriptures from the lecturer Xuanming. At the beginning of the Wanli era, while ill, he went before the Office of the Netherworld.

There, he was summoned for interrogation by the transformed spirit of his enemy, Sheng. Although Zai-de’s case was just, he was initially detained. However, because his principles were upright, he was eventually released.
After observing the release from the dark hells, he returned. Having stayed overnight, the connection was severed again. He saw the spirit of the city moat descend the steps and address him, saying:

"In my previous life, I was a person of Jingzhou, surnamed Cao. Since I ascended the Divine Register, my mother, Lady Zhang, has been reborn three times. Each time she took a female form, she was unable to conceive.

If you would act on my behalf to earnestly entreat a master of profound illumination to reverently recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Candrottarādārikāparipṛcchā Sūtra*, [she may find deliverance]."

Each [recitation] consists of five hundred sections. To save my mother and transform her into a male, the exhortation was most earnest. Reborn through virtue, I respectfully requested the hanging of the lamp.
Having completed the recitation, I submitted the formal petition.
Zhao Bi of Sizhou was traveling to the capital to take the imperial examinations when his wife, Lady Li, had already passed away.

Later, after Bi had attained the jinshi degree and was returning home, he fell into a weary sleep about ten li from his house. He dreamed that his deceased wife was kneeling by the roadside, pleading piteously: "While I was alive..."
The taking of life is an extremely grave offense. Whenever crabs emerge, he would purchase them to make "intoxicated crabs" and eat them to his heart's content.
After death, King Yama ordered that he be driven into the Crab Mountain Hell. There, a swarm of crabs gripped his eyes, causing blood to flow from his entire body.

Day and night he suffers. Furthermore, in his previous life, he spat out the dregs of wine and drank only the residue from the bottom of the cup; he also served as a lowly laborer making rice, congee, and soup.

These were accumulated in the underworld until they reached five *shí*, nine *dǒu*, seven *shēng*, and five *hé*. This caused the slave’s lifespan in the world of the living to be reduced by one *jì* (twelve years).
He must further undergo the sufferings of the thirty-seven great hells. Again, the jailers were commanded to supervise the slave as he sells wine.

I waited until the Ghost of Impermanence arrived to pursue my deceased soul, at which point I drew blood from my own body. It was calculated that five *shí*, nine *dǒu*, seven *shēng*, and five *hé* of blood should be sold;
I vowed to fulfill this original amount, lest I suffer further in hell. Now, hearing that my husband has returned in glory, I have come specifically to plead with you.
The underworld deeply honors those who transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; I beg you to allow me to sell the dowry from my bridal chamber to provide for this purpose.
"Your servant has transcribed seven fascicles. By the merit of this *Prajñāpāramitā*, you may be saved from the sufferings of hell.

When her husband arrived home, he immediately donated his wealth to invite monks to transcribe the scripture. Just as he had completed two fascicles, one day he prepared sacrificial offerings and went to his wife’s grave.
Upon reaching the side of the tomb, he suddenly saw an old man who said, "By virtue of your wife’s merit in transcribing the scripture, she was granted an audience with King Yama at noon yesterday."
"He has already ascended to the heavenly realm. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Shengtian Suichuan and Zhao Wenxin died suddenly in the first year of the Zhenguan era; after three days, they revived. They reported that at the time of their initial death:
Driven away by the officials, the ten companions followed him to the abode of King Yama. Among them was one monk, whom the King first questioned, saying:
"What meritorious deeds did you cultivate while in the world? He replied: "I recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Upon hearing these words, the King immediately rose in alarm, joined his palms, and praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Since you have truly recited the *Prajñā*, you shall surely ascend to heaven. For what reason..."
"I have come here by mistake. Before he had finished speaking, a heavenly robe suddenly descended and led the Master up to heaven.
When Wenxin returned to life, he recounted the matter in full detail.

During the Kaiyuan era, there was a man surnamed Lu who resided in Huazhou. He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One day, while sitting idly during the daylight hours, he saw two men wearing yellow tunics enter his gate.
Lu asked, "Who are you? They replied, "We are the village headmen (*lizheng*). We have come by official decree to summon you. Lu was startled and requested to see the warrant.
Upon opening it, he saw that the seal on top bore the characters for "Wei County," though the writing inside was blurred and indistinct. He did not [read it clearly].

It appeared as if written by a human hand. Finding it strange, he questioned the official. The official replied, "I have received orders to pursue you; I do not know for what reason. Suddenly, he saw the horse at the foot of the steps.
Having no choice, he mounted it and looked back to see the corpse on the bed; he felt deeply loathsome. In his state of agitation, he did not realize it was dead.
He then saw the horse emerge, not through the gate but by traveling along the top of the wall. At this, he was struck with terror and wept.
Only then did he realize she was already dead; he regretted not having been able to bid farewell to his mother and sisters. After traveling some tens of li, he arrived at a city.

The city was most magnificent and grand. He asked, "What city is this? The official replied, "It is the King’s realm. Upon entering the city, he passed through a courtyard and asked, "What courtyard is this?
The official said, "This is the courtyard of the Grand Minister of the Censorate. He then inquired after the Grand Minister’s name and surname, to which the reply was: "His surname is Li."
[Lu]’s name was [So-and-so]. Lu was surprised and delighted, exclaiming, "This is my cousin! He then sent an official to deliver his visiting card.

After a short while, [the other man] came out to meet him with great joy and spoke at length about their past. The Great Officer said to him, "The merit of your younger brother’s recitation of the sutras is truly vast.
This is because the *Vajracchedikā* is the very marrow of the holy teachings; it possesses inconceivable merit. When Lu first entered the monastery, he saw several dozen...
All the people were wearing caps and robes. Later, most of them were bound within nets; some were without clothes, and some had their heads bared. Lu asked, "Who are all these people?
They replied, "These are those from the land of Yang who wore caps and robes. Those within the nets have heavy offenses. If you, my brother, would preach the Dharma for even one of them..."
All who saw him attained rebirth in heaven. He then took the high seat and had Lu ascend it to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Among those within the net, some already began to raise their heads; by the time he reached the middle of the recitation, they all emerged onto the ground—some wearing robes with wide sleeves, others riding in carriages or driving through the clouds.
When the recitation was finished, everyone had been reborn. Upon entering to pay his respects to the King, he was addressed as "Dharma Master. He then...
He was treated with profound courtesy. The King said, "Your merit is inconceivable; even calculation cannot exhaust it. He then ordered his officials to escort him back.

Upon arriving at his home, he saw his family members with disheveled hair, weeping, while his corpse lay upon the ground. His heart was deeply moved by compassion. Suddenly, a maidservant entered from the front of the courtyard;
the official ordered her to follow him up the stairs. As she reached him, his soul suddenly re-entered his body, and he was restored to life.
Gui Xiyan was a leather worker from Jiangxiang City. In his middle years, he abandoned his trade and began carrying offerings of rice and food to Buddhist temples.

Along the way, he single-mindedly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* while simultaneously chanting the name of Amitābha Buddha without ceasing the sound. When he was over sixty years old, he suddenly ceased eating grain.
He drank only water for one month and then declared, "I shall depart on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such a time.

When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. Upon cremating him, several *he* (measures) of *śarīra* relics were obtained; his tongue remained as firm as metal or stone.
When struck, it produced a sound. This occurred during the thirteenth year of the Zhengde era. A butcher from Huzhou named Mr.
Lu was twenty-three years old when he saw a wandering monk before his gate. The monk proclaimed aloud that he was there to convert those with whom he shared a karmic affinity.
Mr. Lu did not understand him, so the monk said, "You have slaughtered countless pigs and sheep; why do you not reform?"

"Karma," Lu said. "You have inherited your ancestral occupation and are unable to renounce it. The monk said, "If you do not reform, in future lives you will surely fall into this same category and be killed by others;
thus, enmity will be requited with enmity, with no time of escape. "I, a poor monk, observe that you possess roots of goodness from past lives.
You should quickly take up the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra. If you uphold them with single-minded devotion, you will then be able to—"
He eliminated his evil karma and increased his merit and virtue. When the monk finished speaking, he vanished from sight. Lu was immediately awakened;

In the *xinchou* year of the Wanli era, Zhang Ai, an eunuch of the Shuncheng Gate, recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in his later years.

When he was on the verge of death, his family members instructed him, saying, "Do not forget your intention to maintain the recitation of the sutra. Ai consented, yet his mouth remained sealed and he could not respond.
He saw two youths dressed in green leading him away, saying, "You shall go to Shandong to take rebirth. His movement was as swift as flight.
By midday, Ai had already reached the eastern mountains. There he beheld the local waters and mountains, as well as his parents from whom he was born.

With single-minded devotion, Ai maintained his recitation of the sutra. They were led by force into a palace hall; Ai suspected it was the Shrine of the Eastern Peak (Mount Tai), yet there were no ox-headed jailers present.

During the Xuande era, the Daoist Chen Ruxuan of Heming Guan in western Sichuan sought longevity with a resolute purpose. He prayed to the deities for the transmission of the Dharma.
One night, he saw a man who called himself the Vajra Deity, who said to Xuan: "Go to Mount Min and pay homage to Master Zhirong; he shall transmit the Dharma to you.
Following these instructions, Xuan went to inquire of him, saying: "I, Xuan, hope for longevity and wish to hear the secret essentials."
Rong said: "Have you not seen the *Vajracchedikā* say that all conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows?
Xuan said: "If they are like illusions and bubbles, what is meant by 'longevity'? Rong said: "If one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata."

He further said, "That which is not the Tathāgata is called the Tathāgata. Xu suddenly attained realization upon hearing these words. He subsequently retired to live in seclusion at Huju Rock on Wagushan.
At the age of ninety-eight, he gathered his neighbors one day and said, "In the beginning, my aspiration was for the immortality of the immortals;

The Discourse on Returning to the One by Layman Gui states: There is a distinction between returning to the West and being reborn in the heavens.
This is because those reborn in the heavens have not yet escaped saṃsāra, whereas returning to the West entails forever departing from birth and death. Why is this so? Saṃsāra consists of six realms.
First is the realm of devas; second, the realm of humans; third, the realm of asuras; fourth, the realm of animals; fifth, the realm of hungry ghosts;
and sixth, the realm of hell. Within these six paths of birth and death, all beings transmigrate without end.
Although receiving blessings in the heavens surpasses that of the human world, their lifespans are nonetheless finite—such as those in the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, and Nirmāṇarati heavens.
The gods of the various heavens have lifespans calculated in thousands; the longest does not exceed several thousand years.

As for the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Māra-kāyika, Ābhāsvara, and Śubhakṛtsna realms, their lifespans are calculated in tens of thousands; even the longest does not exceed several tens of thousands. When their allotted lifespan is exhausted, they pass away.
They still return to take birth in the desire realm and cannot dwell eternally in the heavens; therefore, it is said that they have not yet escaped saṃsāra.
As for the West, beyond ten trillion buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
Its presiding teacher is known as Amitāyus Buddha, who continues to preach the Dharma until this very day. Once one returns to that realm, one shall never again fall back.
It continues to evolve until one attains Buddhahood. The lifespan of such a person is immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation.
As the Sūtra says, when heaven and earth perish, this [state] does not perish; therefore, it is said that one is forever free from birth and death.
Compared to those who are reborn in the heavens, this is not at all different. Furthermore, upholding the Golden Sūtra is equivalent to practicing the Pure Land path.
